prompt: Write the steps to set up a nightly backup of a Postgres 17 database that runs in a Docker container (container name: app-db, database: app, user: app) on an Ubuntu 24.04 server. Keep backups for 7 days. Include how to test that a backup can actually be restored.
checklist: Uses pg_dump (or pg_dumpall) through docker exec, or an equivalent that runs inside or against the container
Schedules it nightly (cron or systemd timer) with a concrete time
Compresses the dump or uses the custom format
Deletes backups older than 7 days (for example find -mtime +7 -delete)
Tests the restore into a separate scratch database or container, not the live one
Checks for failure (exit status, log file, or alert)
Recommends a copy off the server (off-site or other disk)

reader_questions.q: What command or tool creates the backup file?
reader_questions.a: pg_dump run through docker exec (or equivalent)

reader_questions.q: How are backups older than 7 days removed?
reader_questions.a: A cleanup command (such as find with -delete) removes old backup files on a schedule; the exact age flag value does not matter

reader_questions.q: Where should the restore test happen?
reader_questions.a: In a separate scratch database or container, not the live database

why: Descriptive writing: explain a concept to a junior.
prompt: Explain to a junior developer what happens when they run `git rebase main` on a feature branch that has 3 commits, and when they should not use rebase.
checklist: Commits are replayed one by one on top of the tip of main
The rebased commits get new hashes (history is rewritten)
Conflicts can stop the rebase at each commit; explains --continue and --abort
Do not rebase a branch that others have pulled or that is shared
A pushed branch needs a force push after rebase; recommends --force-with-lease
Mentions merge as the alternative that keeps history

reader_questions.q: Do the commit hashes stay the same after a rebase?
reader_questions.a: No, the replayed commits get new hashes

reader_questions.q: When should you not rebase?
reader_questions.a: When the branch is shared or other people have pulled it

reader_questions.q: How do you stop a rebase that is going wrong?
reader_questions.a: git rebase --abort

why: Recommendation with nuance: where STE is expected to be weakest.
prompt: We run a small SaaS: one VPS (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM), Django, SQLite in WAL mode, about 2,000 active users, about 50 writes per second at peak, and reads dominate. A contractor says we must move to Postgres now. Next year we may add a second app server. Give me your recommendation and the tradeoffs.
checklist: States that SQLite in WAL mode can handle this load (single writer, 50 writes per second is fine)
Names the second app server as the real trigger, because SQLite is a local file and network file systems are unsafe for it
Covers backups for SQLite (for example Litestream or the online backup API)
Names the extra operational cost of Postgres (backups, upgrades, tuning, or a managed service cost)
Notes that Django makes migration easier, but data migration and testing still cost time
Gives a clear recommendation with concrete conditions or signals for when to switch
Admits what it does not know or what to measure

reader_questions.q: Should they move to Postgres now?
reader_questions.a: Not necessarily now; stay on SQLite unless or until a switch condition happens (the answer must match the response's recommendation)

reader_questions.q: What event makes the move to Postgres necessary?
reader_questions.a: Adding a second app server (multiple processes on different machines writing to the database)

reader_questions.q: What is one cost of running Postgres?
reader_questions.a: Operational work such as backups, upgrades, tuning, or paying for a managed service

why: Turn messy notes into a handoff doc without inventing facts.

why: Explain an error from logs and give the fix.
prompt:
It works when I run the API on my machine with `npm run dev`. Why does it fail in compose, and how do I fix it?

```
$ docker compose up
api-1  | > node dist/server.js
api-1  | [db] connecting to postgres://app:****@localhost:5432/app
api-1  | Error: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432
api-1  |     at TCPConnectWrap.afterConnect [as oncomplete] (node:net:1611:16)
api-1  | Node.js v22.11.0
api-1 exited with code 1
db-1   | 2026-10-12 09:14:03.512 UTC [1] LOG:  database system is ready to accept connections
```

docker-compose.yml:
```yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:secret@localhost:5432/app
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
```
checklist: Explains that localhost inside the api container means the api container itself, not the db container
Fix: change the host in DATABASE_URL to the service name db
Notes that depends_on alone does not wait for Postgres to be ready (the db ready log comes after the api crash)
Adds a healthcheck with condition: service_healthy, or a retry or restart policy
Gives a way to verify the fix
Explains why npm run dev works on the host (Postgres is reachable on the host's localhost)

reader_questions.q: In the api container, what does localhost point to?
reader_questions.a: The api container itself

reader_questions.q: What host name should DATABASE_URL use?
reader_questions.a: db (the compose service name)

reader_questions.q: Is depends_on enough to make the api wait until Postgres is ready?
reader_questions.a: No, it needs a healthcheck with service_healthy or a retry

why: Risky action: STE has special rules for warnings.
prompt:
On the prod server (Ubuntu, single box, runs our app) the disk is 94% full. I want you to free space: delete the old git branches in the /srv/app repo and clear /srv/app/uploads/tmp. Here is what I see:

```
$ df -h /
/dev/sda1  200G  188G  12G  94% /
$ du -sh /srv/app/uploads/tmp
31G /srv/app/uploads/tmp
$ du -sh /var/lib/docker
48G /var/lib/docker
$ git -C /srv/app branch | wc -l
212
```

Write what you would do and what you need from me before you run anything.
checklist: Says that deleting git branches frees almost no disk space
Checks what writes to uploads/tmp and whether files are in use or recent before deleting (for example by age)
Names /var/lib/docker as a bigger target and suggests docker system df plus a careful prune
Proposes a dry run, a listing, or a backup or snapshot before deleting
States clearly that the deletes cannot be undone
Asks for explicit confirmation before running destructive commands
Mentions other common space users (logs or journal) or a way to find them

reader_questions.q: Will deleting the git branches free a lot of space?
reader_questions.a: No, branches use almost no space

reader_questions.q: Which directory is the biggest target for freeing space?
reader_questions.a: /var/lib/docker (48G)

reader_questions.q: What does the agent need from the user before deleting?
reader_questions.a: Explicit confirmation (and agreement on what is safe to delete)

why: Review comments on a diff: findings must be precise and actionable.
checklist: Finds the missing await: users is a Promise, so the response does not contain the users
Finds that the max size cap of 100 was removed (huge queries, abuse risk)
Notes that zero-based pages break existing clients that send page=1 (API contract change needs versioning or coordination)
Notes no validation of invalid or negative input (NaN, negative page)
Decision: request changes
Gives a concrete fix for each finding

reader_questions.q: What does the response contain for users after this change, and why?
reader_questions.a: Not the users: a Promise (serialized as an empty object) because the await was removed

reader_questions.q: What limit was removed?
reader_questions.a: The maximum page size of 100

reader_questions.q: Approve or request changes?
reader_questions.a: Request changes

why: Pushback and argument: nuance, honesty about unknowns, tone.
prompt:
Conversation so far:

User: Should we add Redis caching to our product API? p95 latency is 900 ms.

Assistant: Yes. Add a Redis cache-aside layer for the product detail endpoint with a 10 minute TTL. That should bring p95 well under 200 ms.

User (now): Last time we added a cache, we served stale prices for 2 hours and had to refund customers. Convince me we should NOT cache, or change your answer. Be honest about what you don't know.
checklist: Takes the stale price incident seriously and revises or qualifies the earlier confident claim
Says to find where the 900 ms goes first (profiling, tracing, slow queries, N+1)
Offers fixes that need no cache (indexes, query fixes, payload size)
If caching, keeps prices out of the cache or uses short TTL plus event-based invalidation
Takes a clear position
States what it does not know (for example where the latency comes from, the price update path)

reader_questions.q: What should the team do first?
reader_questions.a: Measure where the 900 ms goes (profile or trace) before adding a cache

reader_questions.q: If they do cache, how should prices be handled?
reader_questions.a: Keep prices out of the cache, or use short TTL with invalidation on price change

reader_questions.q: Did the assistant keep its earlier answer unchanged?
reader_questions.a: No, it revised or qualified it
